interactions.label: An 8-year-old boy with a femoral shaft fracture is placed in skeletal traction f

params.question: An 8-year-old boy with a femoral shaft fracture is placed in skeletal traction for 8 weeks. Beyond the fracture management, which concern should be the PRIMARY focus of the initial counselling session with his parents?

answers.text: Risk of post-traumatic arthritis in the hip joint

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Post-traumatic arthritis follows intra-articular fractures, not diaphyseal (shaft) fractures. The femoral shaft is not a joint surface injury.

answers.text: Social, financial, and medical complications of prolonged immobilisation, including pressure sores and muscle wasting

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Prolonged traction causes real risks — pressure sores, deep vein thrombosis, infections, and muscle wasting — plus social costs like disrupted schooling and family burden. Early counselling prepares the family to manage these proactively.
Femoral shaft fractures in children heal well with traction; amputation and prosthetics are not relevant here. The concern is the immobilisation period, not limb loss.

answers.text: Genetic testing for hereditary bone fragility disorders

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A traumatic femoral shaft fracture does not indicate a genetic bone disorder. Genetic counselling belongs to the congenital disabilities category, not the prolonged-immobilisation category.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the four categories of prognosis counselling. Prolonged immobilisation carries its own burden: pressure sores, blood clots, muscle wasting, lost income, and family disruption. These must be addressed early.
Well done. Fractures requiring prolonged bed rest or traction demand early counselling about social, financial, and medical complications — not just the fracture itself.

interactions.label: You are counselling a manual labourer after surgery for a comminuted tibial plat

params.question: You are counselling a manual labourer after surgery for a comminuted tibial plateau fracture. He asks whether he will fully recover. Which response BEST demonstrates appropriate prognostic communication?

answers.text: "The surgery was successful, so you should expect a complete recovery."

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Fixing the bone does not guarantee full recovery after an intra-articular fracture. Cartilage damage from the original injury often leads to post-traumatic arthritis regardless of surgical success. This statement offers false reassurance.

answers.text: "You will manage walking at home and light activity, but returning to heavy manual work is unlikely."

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. This ties the prognosis to real functional benchmarks the patient understands. It is honest without being crushing, and preserves hope for achievable goals while setting realistic expectations.

answers.text: "You will never walk normally again; you should prepare for a wheelchair."

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Absolute negative language is inappropriate when meaningful function is preserved. Many tibial plateau fracture patients walk independently — they may not return to heavy labour, but household and light activity are realistic goals.

answers.text: "It is too early to predict anything; recovery depends entirely on your willpower."

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Vague responses that shift responsibility to the patient are neither helpful nor accurate. The orthopaedic team can and should provide a realistic range of functional outcomes based on the injury pattern and surgical findings.

overallFeedback.feedback: For intra-articular fractures, use function-linked language: describe what the patient can realistically expect to do (household walking, light activity) rather than using absolutes, false reassurance, or vague statements.
Excellent. Tying the prognosis to concrete functional milestones — walking, light activity, work capacity — gives the patient an honest and usable picture of the future.

interactions.label: In compartment syndrome, the diagnosis can be excluded if peripheral pulses are

params.question: In compartment syndrome, the diagnosis can be excluded if peripheral pulses are still palpable distal to the injury.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This is false. A palpable pulse does NOT rule out compartment syndrome — pulselessness appears only after irreversible damage has already begun. Among the six P's (pain, pain on passive stretch, pallor, paraesthesia, pulselessness, paralysis), the last two are late and ominous. Pain on passive muscle stretch is the earliest and most reliable sign.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — this statement is false. Pulselessness is a LATE sign in compartment syndrome. Compartment pressure can destroy muscle and nerve tissue while arterial inflow continues. Pain on passive stretching of the affected compartment muscles is the earliest and most reliable clinical sign.

interactions.label: A 60-year-old diabetic patient presents with gangrene limited to the forefoot. D

params.question: A 60-year-old diabetic patient presents with gangrene limited to the forefoot. Doppler studies confirm adequate blood supply to the heel pad and ankle. Which amputation level preserves the MOST function while ensuring adequate healing?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Above-knee amputation sacrifices the knee joint entirely and demands far more energy for prosthetic walking. It is reserved for cases where blood supply above the knee has failed — not appropriate when distal vascularity is intact.

Through-knee disarticulation preserves the femur but unnecessarily sacrifices the ankle and knee function. With a healthy heel pad and adequate ankle vascularity, a more distal level is achievable and preferable.

Below-knee amputation preserves the knee joint and is highly functional, but when gangrene is limited to the forefoot and the heel pad has intact blood supply, a Syme's amputation retains even more function.

Correct. Syme's amputation removes the foot at the ankle while preserving the heel pad for direct weight bearing. It suits limited diabetic gangrene when heel pad vascularity is intact — the most distal level that ensures a viable stump.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember the rule: amputate at the most distal level that ensures healing. With intact heel pad vascularity and limited forefoot gangrene, Syme's amputation preserves the most function while still healing reliably.

Well done. The guiding principle is to amputate at the most distal level that gives a healthy, well-vascularised stump. Syme's amputation with an intact heel pad offers direct weight bearing and maximum preserved function.

interactions.label: A 30-year-old patient is 4 weeks post below-knee amputation. The wound is healin

params.question: A 30-year-old patient is 4 weeks post below-knee amputation. The wound is healing well, but the stump remains oedematous. Which rehabilitation phase is this patient in, and what is the MOST important priority?

answers.text: Preparatory prosthesis phase; begin gait training with a temporary socket

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The preparatory prosthesis phase begins around weeks 6–12, once the stump has healed and started to reduce in volume. At 4 weeks, the stump is still too oedematous for any socket fitting.

answers.text: Pre-prosthetic phase; compression bandaging to reduce stump oedema and exercises to prevent joint contracture

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The first 6 weeks constitute the pre-prosthetic phase. The priorities are wound healing, shrinking stump volume with compression bandaging, and maintaining knee range of motion to prevent flexion contracture — without this groundwork, socket fitting later becomes much harder.

answers.text: Definitive prosthesis phase; fit the permanent prosthesis and train community walking

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The definitive prosthesis is fitted at 3–6 months once the stump shape has stabilised. At 4 weeks, the stump is still actively changing shape and far from ready for a permanent socket.

answers.text: Annual review phase; check the socket fit and inspect stump skin

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Annual reviews begin after the definitive prosthesis is in regular use. At 4 weeks post-amputation, the rehabilitation journey has barely begun.

overallFeedback.feedback: The rehabilitation timeline is: pre-prosthetic phase (0–6 weeks: healing, compression, exercises), preparatory prosthesis (6–12 weeks: temporary socket and early gait), definitive prosthesis (3–6 months), then long-term review. At 4 weeks, the patient is squarely in the pre-prosthetic phase.

Correct. Skipping the pre-prosthetic phase leaves a swollen, cone-shaped stump that cannot be properly fitted with a socket. Compression bandaging and joint exercises in the first 6 weeks lay the foundation for successful prosthetic rehabilitation.
